article:
# Solving two-bidder first-price sealed-bid auctions with ex-ante asymmetry (independent private values): methods, models, and implications

## Executive summary

This report describes the standard mathematical method for solving first-price sealed-bid (FPSB) auctions when two bidders have independent private values drawn from different distributions (ex‑ante asymmetry). It presents the Bayes‑Nash equilibrium characterization, the resulting coupled differential-equation formulation for equilibrium bidding functions, solvable special cases (uniform, symmetric), and practical numerical and approximation methods (shooting/collocation, Taylor-series expansion algorithm, perturbation and boundary-layer techniques). Strategic implications for bidders and the seller (bidding shading, reserve pricing, disclosure, collusion risks) are discussed. Empirical findings and case studies that illustrate how theory performs in practice are summarized. A practical, step‑by‑step procedure for solving a concrete instance is provided, together with recommended references and numerical solution approaches.

Key facts:
- In FPSB with independent private values (IPV), equilibrium bidding strategies are Bayes‑Nash best responses that typically solve a system of coupled nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) when bidders are asymmetric [THEORY LECTURES; NUMERICAL SOLUTIONS]([5](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~mcfadden/eC103_f03/auctionlect.pdf),[3](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2020/07/NumericalSolutions.pdf))[5][3].
- Closed-form solutions exist only in special/symmetric cases (e.g., n symmetric bidders with uniform(0,1) → b(v) = (n−1)/n·v; for two symmetric bidders b(v)=v/2) [Auctions lecture notes]([2](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~marker/stat473-F14/auctions.pdf))[2].
- For asymmetric bidders, numerical solvers, perturbation expansions, and boundary-layer analysis are the standard tools; specialized algorithms based on local Taylor-series expansions are effective and robust in practice [Numerical Solutions; Perturbation papers]([3](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2020/07/NumericalSolutions.pdf),[7](http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~fibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf))[3][7].
- Empirical work finds substantial bid shading (experiment averages often well below valuations) and real-world asymmetries materially affect allocation, profits and revenue (procurement, oil leases, etc.) [Experimental and empirical studies]([19](https://www.dbc.wroc.pl/Content/122687/Kusmierczyk_First-price_sealed-bid_auction.pdf),[17](https://users.ssc.wisc.edu/~hendrick/publications/EmpiricalStudyofAuction.pdf))[19][17].

## 1. Model setup and equilibrium concept

Model assumptions (standard IPV framework)
- Single indivisible object for sale.
- Two bidders i = 1,2. Bidder i’s private valuation Vi is drawn independently from continuous distribution Fi on support Ti = [vi,min, vi,max] with density fi. Distributions Fi may differ across bidders (ex‑ante asymmetry).
- Bids are sealed and simultaneous. Highest bidder wins and pays own bid (first-price). Ties are broken by a predetermined rule (irrelevant except on measure-zero sets).
- Bidders are risk neutral (extensions to risk aversion are discussed below).
- Common knowledge: each bidder knows its own Fi and the opponent’s distribution Fj, and that the opponent plays an increasing bidding strategy (standard equilibrium assumption).

Equilibrium concept
- A Bayes‑Nash equilibrium (BNE) is a pair of measurable, monotone increasing bidding functions b1(v) and b2(v) such that for every vi, bi(vi) maximizes expected payoff given the opponent’s bidding function.
- Expected payoff for bidder i with value v who submits bid b is:
  U_i(b; v) = (v − b) · P(win | b),
  where P(win | b) = P(b ≥ b_j(V_j)) = F_j(b_j^{-1}(b)) when b_j is strictly increasing and invertible.
- First-order conditions for interior optimum yield the equilibrium characterization (next section).

References: basic description of FPSB and BNE for IPV auctions [Auctions - ComLabGames]([1](http://comlabgames.com/47-901/lectures/1%20Sealed%20Bid%20Auctions.pdf)) and standard lecture notes [Auctions First Price Sealed Bid Auctions]([2](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~marker/stat473-F14/auctions.pdf))[1][2].

## 2. Deriving the equilibrium: first-order condition and coupled ODEs

Sketch of derivation (two bidders)

1. Fix bidder 2’s increasing strategy b2(.). Consider bidder 1 with value v1. If bidder 1 bids b, she wins iff b ≥ b2(v2) ⇔ v2 ≤ b2^{-1}(b). So the win probability is F2(b2^{-1}(b)). Her expected payoff:
   U1(b; v1) = (v1 − b) · F2(b2^{-1}(b)).

2. First-order condition (interior optimum): differentiate U1 w.r.t. b and set to zero:
   dU1/db = −F2(b2^{-1}(b)) + (v1 − b) · f2(b2^{-1}(b)) · (d/d b) b2^{-1}(b) = 0.

   Using (d/d b) b2^{-1}(b) = 1 / b2'( b2^{-1}(b) ), the FOC becomes
   F2(w2) = (v1 − b) · f2(w2) / b2'(w2),
   where w2 = b2^{-1}(b).

3. Evaluate this identity at equilibrium b = b1(v1) and w2 = b2^{-1}(b1(v1)). Replace v1 with the argument of b1 on left side through invertibility to obtain a differential equation linking b1 and b2. Doing the symmetric derivation for bidder 2 yields a system of two coupled first-order nonlinear ODEs for b1(.), b2(.).

4. The system requires boundary conditions. Standard conditions usually used:
   - At the lower bound v = vmin_i, bidder i bids b_i(vmin_i) = vmin_i (or sometimes equals reservation-bid condition depending on support). For continuous supports starting at 0, often b_i(0)=0. Practically, use natural boundary condition derived from FOC or the requirement of no profitable deviation at the lower support endpoint.

Key point
- The equilibrium characterization is a pair of coupled ODEs. Except for very simple distributions (e.g., symmetric uniform), these ODEs do not admit closed-form solutions and must be solved numerically or approximated analytically [Numerical Solutions; Perturbation]([3](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2020/07/NumericalSolutions.pdf),[7](http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~fibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf))[3][7].

References for the formal derivation and existence/uniqueness issues: detailed treatments and equations in McFadden lecture notes and a dedicated numerical methods paper [THEORY LECTURES; NUMERICAL SOLUTIONS]([5](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~mcfadden/eC103_f03/auctionlect.pdf),[3](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2020/07/NumericalSolutions.pdf))[5][3].

## 3. Solvable special cases (closed-form results)

Symmetric independent private values (iid) — general formula
- For n symmetric bidders with common CDF F on support [vmin, vmax], the symmetric equilibrium bidding function b(v) (increasing) satisfies:
  b(v) = v − ∫_{vmin}^v F(x)^{n−1} dx / F(v)^{n−1}.
- For two symmetric bidders (n = 2): b(v) = v − ∫_{vmin}^v F(x) dx / F(v).
- Uniform(0,1) and two bidders: F(x)=x, so b(v) = v − (v^2/2)/v = v/2. More generally, with n symmetric bidders uniform(0,1): b(v) = (n−1)/n · v [Auctions lecture notes]([2](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~marker/stat473-F14/auctions.pdf))[2].

Asymmetric special-case closed forms
- Explicit closed-form solutions for asymmetric two-bidder IPV FPSB are exceptional. If distributions are simple transforms of each other, or if one bidder’s distribution degenerates, closed forms can sometimes be obtained, but in general one must use numeric or approximation methods [Numerical Solutions; Perturbation]([3](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2020/07/NumericalSolutions.pdf),[7](http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~fibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf))[3][7].

References for symmetric closed forms and revenue equivalence: standard lecture notes and auctions surveys [Auctions First Price Sealed Bid Auctions; Revenue Equivalence overviews]([2](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~marker/stat473-F14/auctions.pdf),[4](https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/Auctions.html))[2][4].

## 4. Numerical and analytical solution methods for asymmetric cases

Because the equilibrium ODE system is generally not solvable in closed form, standard solution approaches include:

A. Numerical methods (general-purpose)
- Shooting methods: treat unknown boundary values and 'shoot' to match terminal condition. Sensitive to initial guesses.
- Collocation and discretization: discretize the interval and solve the nonlinear system for values b_i(v_k) at grid points (e.g., collocation, finite differences, pseudospectral methods).
- Use of monotonicity and continuation methods to improve convergence.

Practical implementation and robust algorithm
- A fully automated algorithm based on local Taylor-series expansions and algebraic manipulations is available to compute inverse equilibrium bid functions for general user-supplied distributions; it is numerically robust and handles tabulated distributions [Numerical Solutions]([3](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2020/07/NumericalSolutions.pdf))[3].

B. Perturbation methods (analytical approximations)
- Expand around a symmetric baseline: write Fi = F + ε·Hi and expand bidding functions b_i = b^0 + ε·b^1 + ... . Solve the sequence of linear problems for correction terms. This yields explicit approximations when asymmetry is small [Asymmetric Perturbation papers]([7](http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~fibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf),[10](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/moor.28.4.836.20510))[7][10].

C. Boundary-layer and singular-perturbation analysis
- For large asymmetry (one bidder much stronger), solutions may develop boundary layers (sharp changes) near support endpoints. Specialized boundary-layer analysis yields approximations and clarifies limiting behavior [Large Asymmetric — boundary-layer]([6](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/140968811))[6].

D. Heuristic and approximate strategies
- Conditional Second Value (CSV): bidders bid the expected maximum rival valuation conditional on it being below their own value. CSV can be used as a heuristic; however, CSV is not in general an equilibrium bidding function in asymmetric FPSB [Auction Theory lecture notes]([5](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~mcfadden/eC103_f03/auctionlect.pdf))[5].

Recommended practical approach
1. Try analytic solution only in symmetric or very simple distribution cases.
2. For general asymmetric Fi, use the specialized numerical algorithm based on Taylor expansions or discretize and solve the coupled ODE system numerically [Numerical Solutions]([3](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2020/07/NumericalSolutions.pdf))[3].
3. Use perturbation expansions if asymmetry is small to obtain closed-form approximations and intuition [Asymmetric Perturbation]([7](http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~fibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf))[7].
4. Validate numerics by best-response checks and Monte Carlo simulation of the equilibrium.

References for algorithms and perturbation/boundary-layer analyses: [Numerical Solutions of Asymmetric FPSB] and [Asymmetric First-Price Auctions—A Perturbation Approach / Boundary-layer work]([3](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2020/07/NumericalSolutions.pdf),[7](http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~fibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf),[6](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/140968811))[3][7][6].

## 5. Strategic implications and bidder/auctioneer strategies

Implications for bidders
- Bid shading: In FPSB bidders typically bid below true valuation to balance winning probability and payment. The amount of shading depends on the distribution of rivals’ values and the number/strength of rivals [Auctions lecture notes]([2](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~marker/stat473-F14/auctions.pdf))[2].
- Strong vs weak bidders: A stronger bidder (distribution more concentrated toward higher values) benefits more from being strong; asymmetry alters optimal shading patterns and relative payoffs [Brock & others]([8](https://brocku.ca/repec/pdf/0504.pdf))[8].
- Knowledge of opponent’s distribution matters: Asymmetry in information or beliefs about rivals can lead to inefficient allocation and affect revenue [Andreoni et al., asymmetric information about rivals]([15](http://www.columbia.edu/~yc2271/files/publications/chekim.pdf))[15].
- Risk aversion and budgets: Risk aversion leads to more aggressive bidding (less shading). Budget constraints can produce multiple equilibria and stratification by budget [Budget-constrained FPSB]([3](https://econtheory.org/ojs/index.php/te/article/viewFile/20200199/26189/758))[3].

Implications for auction designers (seller)
- Revenue and efficiency:
  - Revenue equivalence: Under standard regularity assumptions, many auction formats yield same expected revenue (with certain caveats). Deviations arise under asymmetry, risk aversion, and budget constraints [Revenue Equivalence theorem discussions]([4](https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/Auctions.html))[4].
  - Asymmetry often reduces allocative efficiency and can either increase or decrease seller revenue depending on specifics: e.g., strong bidders prefer second‑price auctions while weak bidders prefer first‑price auctions; auctioneer’s revenue ranking can change with asymmetry [Auction design comparisons]([19](https://anderson-review.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Ngangoue_Kathleen_The_Common_Probability_Auction_Puzzle.pdf))[19].
- Reserve pricing and entry: Asymmetric reserve prices (or tailored mechanisms) can increase revenue [Asymmetric reserve price literature]([10](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/moor.28.4.836.20510))[10].
- Information disclosure: The level of transparency and disclosure about rivals affects bidding and can change seller revenue and efficiency; disclosure policies should account for strategic responses to asymmetric information [Procurement transparency literature]([11](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00207543.2025.2582764?src=))[11].
- Collusion and ex-ante agreements: Ex-ante collusion possibilities change outcomes; auction rules and monitoring influence collusion incentives [Limits of auctions under ex-ante collusion]([12](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm/5231187.pdf?abstractid=5231187&mirid=1))[12].

Strategic heuristics and practical bidding rules
- Compute best-response shading given estimate of opponent’s CDF and guessed bid function; iteratively update via simulation to approximate BNE.
- Use CSV or related conditional expectations for initial heuristics; refine numerically.
- Consider risk aversion: more risk‑averse bidders reduce shading (bid closer to value).

References: papers on bidder asymmetries, risk aversion and budget constraints, strategic effects of information asymmetry [Bidder asymmetries & budgets; Risk aversion review]([3](https://econtheory.org/ojs/index.php/te/article/viewFile/20200199/26189/758),[15](http://www.columbia.edu/~yc2271/files/publications/chekim.pdf),[16](https://www.aporc.org/LNOR/10/ISORA2009F50.pdf))[3][15][16].

## 6. Empirical evidence and illustrative case studies

Key empirical and experimental findings
- Experimental evidence often shows substantial bid shading relative to valuation. In one lab study, the sealed-bid phase produced bids averaging about 85.8% of valuations, implying substantial but not full shading [Sealed-bid experiments]([19](https://www.dbc.wroc.pl/Content/122687/Kusmierczyk_First-price_sealed-bid_auction.pdf))[19].
- Procurement auctions with asymmetric bidders (e.g., neighbor vs. non-neighbor firms winning drainage tracts) show asymmetric information and coordination can lead to strong bidders capturing rents while weaker bidders get zero or close to zero profits [Empirical study of asymmetric auction]([17](https://users.ssc.wisc.edu/~hendrick/publications/EmpiricalStudyofAuction.pdf))[17].
- Procurement and toxic asset auctions: asymmetric information affects bidding behavior and auction outcomes; auction rules (compensation for over-supply, multiple phases) materially shift bids and profits [Procurement auction studies]([16](https://www.aporc.org/LNOR/10/ISORA2009F50.pdf),[9](https://kylewoodward.com/blog-data/pdfs/references/amann+leininger-games-and-economic-behavior-1996A.pdf))[16][9].

Case study highlights
- Oil and mineral tract auctions: neighbor firms with superior local information won most profitable tracts and captured significant surplus; asymmetry and possible coordination explained observed patterns [Empirical Study of an Auction with Asymmetric Information]([17](https://users.ssc.wisc.edu/~hendrick/publications/EmpiricalStudyofAuction.pdf))[17].
- Procurement design experiments: adding negotiation phases or information changes can lower final prices relative to standard FPSB outcomes, contrary to some naive expectations [Procurement auction experiments]([19](https://www.dbc.wroc.pl/Content/122687/Kusmierczyk_First-price_sealed-bid_auction.pdf))[19].

References for empirical studies and experimental evidence: [Kusmierczyk], [Hendrick empirical study], and surveys [Empirical perspective on auctions]([19](https://www.dbc.wroc.pl/Content/122687/Kusmierczyk_First-price_sealed-bid_auction.pdf),[17](https://users.ssc.wisc.edu/~hendrick/publications/EmpiricalStudyofAuction.pdf),[12](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~webfac/cshannon/e208_sp08/cheng.pdf))[19][17][12].

## 7. Practical step-by-step procedure to solve a concrete two-bidder asymmetric instance

Given Fi, fi for i = 1,2, and supports Ti:

1. Check assumptions: continuous densities, supports known, monotone increasing candidate bids are reasonable.
2. Attempt analytic solution:
   - If Fi are identical (symmetric), use symmetric formula b(v) = v − ∫ F^{n−1}/F^{n−1} for n=2 (often yields closed form).
   - If non-identical but simple transforms exist, test for closed-form simplifications.
3. If no analytic solution:
   a. Set up the equilibrium FOC for each bidder as in Section 2 to obtain the coupled ODE system.
   b. Choose boundary conditions: typically b_i(vmin_i)=vmin_i (or zero if supports begin at 0), and ensure monotonicity.
   c. Choose a solution method:
      - Use a robust prepared solver such as the Taylor-series-based algorithm (see [Numerical Solutions]) if available.
      - Otherwise discretize the support and solve the nonlinear system for b_i at grid points (collocation or Newton methods).
      - For mild asymmetry, compute a perturbation around a symmetric solution.
      - For large asymmetry, use boundary-layer approximations to guide initial guesses.
   d. Verify numerically that each b_i is a best response by sampling values and computing expected payoffs against the opponent’s computed strategy (best-response check).
4. Conduct sensitivity analysis:
   - Vary distribution parameters, risk aversion, or reserve prices to see how equilibrium bids and seller revenue change.
   - Use Monte Carlo simulation to estimate expected revenue, allocation efficiency, and bidder profits under computed equilibrium.
5. For policy design:
   - Evaluate default FPSB revenue vs. alternatives (reserve prices, second-price, disclosure rules).
   - Consider asymmetric reserve or mechanism design if asymmetry is known and significant.

Tools and implementation tips
- Use high-precision ODE solvers and robust root-finding (Newton-Kantorovich, trust-region).
- Use continuation in asymmetry parameter ε (start from symmetric solution and slowly increase ε).
- Validate against known benchmarks (uniform symmetric b(v)=v/2).
- For empirical calibration, estimate Fi from historical bid/value data or use structural estimation methods (see empirical auction literature).

Reference for a ready numerical approach and implementation discussion: [Numerical Solutions of Asymmetric, First-Price, Independent Private Values]([3](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2020/07/NumericalSolutions.pdf))[3].

## 8. Extensions and caveats

- Risk aversion: changes FOC and reduces bid shading (bids closer to valuation). Analysis requires replacing expected payoff with expected utility (u(v − b)), and ODEs become more complex; no closed-form general solution [Risk aversion literature]([15](https://shoshanavasserman.com/files/2021/05/RiskAversionSurvey.pdf))[15].
- Budget constraints: introduce non-convexities, multiple equilibria, and stratification by budgets [Budget-constrained FPSB]([3](https://econtheory.org/ojs/index.php/te/article/viewFile/20200199/26189/758))[3].
- Common-value components: the IPV assumption is crucial for the analysis above. With common values or affiliated signals, winners’ curse considerations alter optimal bidding dramatically and require different equilibria frameworks [Common-value auction literature]([16](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~webfac/cshannon/e208_sp08/cheng.pdf))[16].
- Information structure: if bidders have heterogeneous information about rivals’ types (beyond distributional asymmetry), outcomes may be inefficient and unpredictable; designs must consider bidder-specific information asymmetries [Andreoni et al.; Che-Kim?]([15](http://www.columbia.edu/~yc2271/files/publications/chekim.pdf),[6](http://www.columbia.edu/~yc2271/files/publications/chekim.pdf))[15][6].
- Collusion and strategic entry: practical auction implementation should consider collusion-proofness and entry incentives [Collusion literature]([12](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm/5231187.pdf?abstractid=5231187&mirid=1))[12].

## 9. Recommendations for practitioners

For analysts solving or simulating a two-bidder asymmetric FPSB with IPV:
- Start with careful estimation of bidders’ Fi (empirical calibration).
- If asymmetry is small, use perturbation approximations to obtain quick analytic intuition.
- Otherwise, use robust numerical algorithms (Taylor-series-based algorithm or collocation) and validate with best-response checks.
- Use simulation to assess seller revenue and efficiency under alternative auction rules (reserve pricing, disclosure).
- Consider risk aversion and budget constraints if realistic for application; incorporate into the numerical model.
- Monitor for empirical signatures of collusion or coordinated bidding in field applications.

## Conclusion

Two-bidder FPSB auctions with independent private values and ex‑ante asymmetry lead to coupled nonlinear ODEs that rarely admit closed-form equilibrium strategies except in simple symmetric cases. The standard solution method is to derive the equilibrium first-order conditions and solve the resulting system using numerical methods, perturbation expansions, or boundary-layer techniques depending on the degree and type of asymmetry. Strategic consequences (bid shading, allocation inefficiency, revenue effects) are significant and must inform both bidder strategy and auction design. Empirical and experimental evidence supports substantial bid shading and shows that asymmetries materially affect outcomes in real auctions (procurement, resource leases, etc.). Robust numerical tools and careful empirical calibration are essential for applying theory to practice.

article:
# Mitigating plasma‑etch damage to lithium niobate (LN) for nonlinear photonics

## Executive summary
Plasma etching of lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN) is essential for high‑index‑contrast integrated nonlinear photonic devices but commonly induces surface amorphization, stoichiometry changes, non‑volatile by‑product redeposition (notably LiF), sidewall roughness, mask erosion and subsurface damage that increase optical loss and reduce nonlinear efficiency. Effective mitigation requires a combined approach: select etch chemistries and process parameters that limit non‑volatile residue and physical sputter damage; use directional, low‑redeposition etch methods (including ALE variants); protect and optimize masks and patterning; apply post‑etch chemical and thermal treatments (wet cleans, CMP, high‑temperature anneals, surface passivation) to remove residue and repair defects; and validate with targeted metrology and device tests. The following sections summarize mechanisms, detailed strategies, practical recipes and recommended characterization methods with references.

## Damage mechanisms during LN plasma etching
- Chemical reaction by‑products: Fluorine‑based chemistries (SF6, CF4) readily form LiF, a non‑volatile salt that redeposits on sidewalls and masks, causing rough, tapered profiles, ARDE and low etch rates [Redeposition‑free inductively‑coupled plasma etching of lithium ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/) [1], [Advanced Etching Techniques of LiNbO3 Nanodevices - PMC - NIH](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/) [2].
- Physical sputtering and ion damage: High ion energy/biased plasmas cause amorphization, point defects and subsurface disorder that increase optical absorption and scatter [High‑Quality Dry Etching of LiNbO3 Assisted by Proton Substitution ...](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-4991/12/16/2836) [3].
- Crystallographic anisotropy: Etch rates and damage differ by crystal face; the −Z face etches faster and displays different morphology than +Z and X/Y faces, creating orientation‑dependent roughness and etch uniformity issues [Applications of thin‑film lithium niobate ...](https://www.spiedigitallibrary.org/journals/advanced-photonics/volume-4/issue-03/034001/Applications-of-thin-film-lithium-niobate-in-nonlinear-integrated-photonics/10.1117/1.AP.4.3.034001.full) [5].
- Charging and ferroelectric domains: Polar surfaces and ferroelectric domains can concentrate charge during plasma exposure, enhancing local ion bombardment effects and micro‑cracking [Lithium niobate on insulator: an emerging nanophotonic crystal ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11571947/) [11].
- Temperature dependence: Substrate temperature strongly affects etch rate and morphology; heating can increase etch rate and improve sidewall quality in some chemistries but may also accelerate unwanted reactions or redeposition if not controlled [The effect of a lithium niobate heating on the etching rate in SF6 ICP ...](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf) [4].

## Etch‑process strategies to minimize damage
Practical mitigation begins in the etch tool and recipe. Key levers:

### 1) Choose chemistry that avoids non‑volatile Li compounds or produces volatile by‑products
- Use bromine‑based or chlorine/bromine hybrid chemistries (HBr/BCl3/Ar) or Br‑rich plasmas for better volatility of Li‑containing products; Br chemistries yield fewer non‑volatile residues and reduce redeposition versus F chemistries [Redeposition‑free inductively‑coupled plasma etching of lithium ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/) [1], [Directional atomic layer etching of MgO‑doped lithium niobate using ... (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.10592v2) [9].
- If F‑based gases are used, add gases (O2) or use process conditions that suppress LiF redeposition (elevated substrate temperature, proper pressure and bias to enhance desorption or sputter‑remove LiF) [The effect of a lithium niobate heating on the etching rate in SF6 ICP ...](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf) [4], [Advanced Etching Techniques of LiNbO3 Nanodevices - PMC - NIH](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/) [2].

### 2) Reduce redeposition through tool and parameter control
- Operate in a redeposition‑free regime: optimize chamber pressure, ICP power, and RF/ DC bias so by‑products are pumped away and not recondensed. Higher DC bias and certain pressure windows reduce redeposition for LN ICP etches [Redeposition‑free inductively‑coupled plasma etching of lithium ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/) [1].
- Add inert sputter gas (Ar) in controlled amounts to aid physical removal of LiF but balance to avoid excessive substrate sputtering [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/) [2].

### 3) Use directional, low‑damage etch modes (ALE / directional ALE)
- Directional atomic layer etching (ALE) schemes that alternate chemical modification and low‑energy argon removal steps can produce vertical profiles without heavy ion bombardment and avoid ARDE; recently demonstrated HBr/BCl3/Ar ALE processes produced high fidelity nanostructures with minimal redeposition [Directional atomic layer etching of MgO‑doped lithium niobate using ... (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.10592v2) [9], [Redeposition‑free inductively‑coupled plasma etching of lithium ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/) [1].

### 4) Control substrate temperature strategically
- Moderate substrate heating (several 100 °C) can increase etch rates and improve smoothness in SF6/O2 chemistries by promoting volatile product formation and desorption; however, temperature must be tuned to avoid enhanced redeposition or mask delamination [The effect of a lithium niobate heating on the etching rate in SF6 ICP ...](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf) [4].

### 5) Select and engineer hard masks and sacrificial layers
- Use high‑selectivity, low‑erosion hard masks (e.g., thick SiO2, Al, Cr, or evaporated/ LPCVD Si) or multi‑layer metal + dielectric stacks to protect LN and maintain pattern fidelity. Mask erosion leads to extra milling of LN and increases roughness [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/) [2].
- Poly‑Si trap layers or conductive cap layers can reduce parasitic conduction and charging that exacerbates plasma damage in devices [Redeposition‑free inductively‑coupled plasma etching of lithium ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/) [1].

### 6) Minimize ion energy and exposure time
- Reduce RF bias and use pulsed plasma or lower energy ion bombardment where possible to limit subsurface amorphization, then rely more on selective chemistry/ALE for material removal [High‑Quality Dry Etching of LiNbO3 Assisted by Proton Substitution ...](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-4991/12/16/2836) [3].

## Post‑etch treatments and surface restoration
Combining appropriate post‑etch cleaning and thermal processing recovers optical quality and reduces defects.

### 1) Wet chemical cleaning to remove residues and redeposits
- Buffered HF (BOE), HF dips, and SC‑1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) and SC‑2 cleans can dissolve or loosen Li‑rich or non‑volatile residues; application must be tuned to avoid undercutting or delamination of patterned layers (thin film LNOI surfaces are particularly sensitive) [Thin film LiNbO3 surface preparation using SC‑1](https://opg.optica.org/ome/abstract.cfm?uri=ome-15-11-2826) [7], [Integrated Lithium‑Niobate Nonlinear Photonics Enabled by Wet ...](https://profiles.wustl.edu/en/publications/integrated-lithium-niobate-nonlinear-photonics-enabled-by-wet-etc-2) [6].
- Rinsing and controlled drying (e.g., IPA and N2 blow, critical point dry for delicate structures) to avoid stiction or water marks.

### 2) Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP)
- Gentle CMP can remove a thin, damage‑rich surface layer and improve roughness after etch; useful for larger features or when pattern geometry allows CMP access [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/) [2].

### 3) High‑temperature annealing (thermal anneal, RTA)
- High‑temperature anneals (several hundred °C to 500–800 °C depending on stack compatibility) reduce subsurface disorder, heal ion‑damage, decrease oxygen vacancies and lower optical absorption. Pre‑ and post‑annealing have been shown to improve proton‑exchanged waveguide homogeneity and optical characteristics; optimal temperatures reported near ~500 °C for some processes [Effect of pre‑annealing of lithium niobate on the structure ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0925346718307535) [16], [Integrated Lithium‑Niobate Nonlinear Photonics Enabled by Wet ...](https://profiles.wustl.edu/en/publications/integrated-lithium-niobate-nonlinear-photonics-enabled-by-wet-etc-2) [6].
- Anneal ambient matters: oxygen or forming gas (N2/H2) can affect surface stoichiometry and vacancy populations; oxygen anneal helps restore stoichiometry and reduce color centers.

### 4) Plasma‑based post treatments (gentle)
- Low‑power oxygen plasma can remove organic residues and re‑oxidize the surface; controlled O2 plasma can also tune surface stoichiometry and reduce defect‑related absorption if not overdone [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/) [2].
- Avoid aggressive ion‑rich plasmas that reintroduce damage.

### 5) Surface passivation and dielectric capping
- Atomic layer deposition (ALD) of conformal dielectrics (Al2O3, SiO2, SiN) provides chemical passivation, reduces surface states and protects from environmental degradation. Thin passivation layers can also reduce scatter and provide a stable refractive index environment [Applications of thin‑film lithium niobate ...](https://www.spiedigitallibrary.org/journals/advanced-photonics/volume-4/issue-03/034001/Applications-of-thin-film-lithium-niobate-in-nonlinear-integrated-photonics/10.1117/1.AP.4.3.034001.full) [5].
- For electro‑optic devices choose passivation that does not screen the applied fields excessively.

### 6) Proton substitution and restoration strategies
- Proton exchange has been used to assist etching or bonding; post‑process thermal treatments may be required to re‑distribute protons or restore crystal order to minimize optical loss [High‑Quality Dry Etching of LiNbO3 Assisted by Proton Substitution ...](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-4991/12/16/2836) [3], [Plasma etching of proton‑exchanged lithium niobate](https://pubs.aip.org/avs/jva/article/24/4/1012/102827/) [8].

## Device/process flow recommendations (practical recipe)
The following is a practical, conservative flow to etch LN for low‑loss nonlinear photonics:

1. Substrate preparation
   - Start with high‑quality LNOI/TFLN wafers; perform pre‑clean (solvent, piranha or SC‑1 depending on stack) to remove organics; avoid SC‑1 overexposure if thin films are present [Thin film LiNbO3 surface preparation using SC‑1](https://opg.optica.org/ome/abstract.cfm?uri=ome-15-11-2826) [7].
2. Masking
   - Deposit a thick hard mask (SiO2, Si, or metal stack); pattern with optimized lithography; consider a thin conductive layer to reduce charging.
3. Etch: directional, low‑redeposition ICP or ALE
   - Use bromine‑based or HBr/BCl3/Ar chemistry and tune chamber pressure/ICP power to redeposition‑free regime (see parameter window studies) [Redeposition‑free inductively‑coupled plasma etching of lithium ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/) [1].
   - Use low RF bias and, if available, directional ALE (chemical modification + low‑energy Ar removal) to produce vertical, smooth sidewalls [Directional atomic layer etching ... (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.10592v2) [9].
   - Maintain moderate substrate heating when beneficial (SF6/O2 showed improved quality at elevated T, but avoid conditions that promote LiF redeposition) [The effect of a lithium niobate heating on the etching rate in SF6 ICP ...](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf) [4].
4. Immediate post‑etch wet clean
   - Rinse in DI; perform controlled SC‑1 (if compatible) or BOE/HF dips to remove residues; monitor for under‑etch/delamination risk [Integrated Lithium‑Niobate Nonlinear Photonics Enabled by Wet ...](https://profiles.wustl.edu/en/publications/integrated-lithium-niobate-nonlinear-photonics-enabled-by-wet-etc-2) [6], [Thin film LiNbO3 surface preparation using SC‑1](https://opg.optica.org/ome/abstract.cfm?uri=ome-15-11-2826) [7].
5. Gentle oxygen plasma (optional)
   - Short, low‑power O2 plasma to strip organics and re‑oxidize the surface.
6. Thermal anneal
   - Anneal in oxygen (or controlled ambient) at a temperature compatible with device stack (often 350–600 °C; some studies up to 500–800 °C for proton‑exchanged structures) to heal damage and reduce vacancy concentration. Optimize time and ramp to avoid delamination [Effect of pre‑annealing of lithium niobate on the structure ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0925346718307535) [16].
7. Final surface passivation
   - Deposit a thin ALD Al2O3 or SiO2/SiN passivation to stabilize surface states and protect the device for subsequent processing [Applications of thin‑film lithium niobate ...](https://www.spiedigitallibrary.org/journals/advanced-photonics/volume-4/issue-03/034001/Applications-of-thin-film-lithium-niobate-in-nonlinear-integrated-photonics/10.1117/1.AP.4.3.034001.full) [5].

## Tradeoffs and practical considerations
- Chemistry tradeoffs: Bromine chemistries reduce LiF but can etch harder mask materials faster and may produce different sidewall profiles; F‑based processes may give higher selectivity for some masks but suffer LiF redeposition [Redeposition‑free inductively‑coupled plasma etching of lithium ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/) [1].
- Temperature tradeoffs: Higher substrate temperature often increases etch rates and smoothness in some gases, but can exacerbate mask delamination or recondensation of by‑products if pumping is insufficient [The effect of a lithium niobate heating on the etching rate in SF6 ICP ...](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf) [4].
- Device performance vs process complexity: ALE and multi‑step post‑processes yield the best optical quality but increase cycle time and process complexity; weigh against device Q and yield targets [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/) [2].
- Film vs bulk: Thin‑film LNOI requires gentler handling (SC‑1 sensitivity, thin buried oxide, bonding layers) compared to bulk LN [Thin film LiNbO3 surface preparation using SC‑1](https://opg.optica.org/ome/abstract.cfm?uri=ome-15-11-2826) [7].

## Characterization and verification
Routine characterization after process changes is essential:
- Optical loss / Q factor measurements of resonators and waveguides to quantify propagation loss and nonlinear conversion efficiency [High density lithium niobate photonic integrated circuits](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-40502-8) [12].
- AFM for surface roughness and sidewall morphology [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/) [2].
- Cross‑section TEM to inspect subsurface amorphous layers and mask interface.
- XPS / SIMS for surface stoichiometry and Li, F, or Br residue detection.
- Raman and optical absorption spectroscopy to detect color centers and defect states.
- Electrical/ferroelectric domain imaging if domain integrity is critical.

## Recommended experimental plan to optimize a specific recipe
1. Baseline: etch a test matrix across chemistry (HBr vs SF6/O2), pressure, ICP power, RF bias, substrate temperature and mask type. Measure etch rate, profile, roughness and residues.
2. Select low‑redeposition window per tool (pump speed, pressure) and confirm with SEM/XPS.
3. Compare conventional ICP vs ALE directional runs for target feature sizes (<200 nm gaps to µm trenches).
4. For best recipes, apply post‑etch wet clean + anneal and measure optical Q and stoichiometry changes.
5. Iterate mask stacks and passivation to reach device performance targets.

## Conclusion
Mitigating plasma etch damage in LN requires integrated optimization across chemistry, etch physics, masking and post‑process repair. The most effective strategies combine (1) choosing low‑redeposition chemistries (Br‑based or tuned F‑based with O2 and heat), (2) operating in a redeposition‑free ICP or using directional ALE to minimize ion damage, (3) robust mask and charge‑management layers, and (4) post‑etch aqueous/chemical cleaning, CMP where feasible, and high‑temperature anneals plus passivation to heal damage and stabilize surfaces. Systematic metrology and device performance testing close the loop and allow recipes to be tailored to the device architecture (thin‑film LNOI vs bulk, polar face orientation, presence of proton‑exchanged layers). Implementing these combined approaches has enabled recent demonstrations of low‑loss, high‑density LN photonic circuits and robust nonlinear devices [Redeposition‑free inductively‑coupled plasma etching of lithium ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/) [1], [High density lithium niobate photonic integrated circuits](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-40502-8) [12].

prompt: Write an analysis exploring how historical narratives are being reinterpreted through contemporary political and social lenses. Focus on areas like ideologisation of history, instrumentalisation of the past and efforts to reclaim silenced narratives. Analyze how commemorative practices shape historiography and how historical memory serves current agendas. Please provide relevant examples and scholarly perspectives.
article:
# Reinterpreting the Past: Ideologisation, Reclamation, and Commemoration in Contemporary Historical Narratives

## Introduction: scope and key questions
Historical narratives are not neutral records of the past but contested resources that actors use to make sense of the present and to pursue political, social, and cultural goals. This report examines three interrelated dynamics:
- The ideologisation and instrumentalisation of history (how past events are framed to support current agendas);
- Efforts to reclaim silenced or marginalized narratives (restorative and corrective work by scholars, communities, and technologies); and
- The role of commemorative practices (monuments, memorials, anniversaries, curricula) in shaping public historiography and collective memory.

The analysis draws on scholarly literature, policy-oriented reports, and documented case studies to show mechanisms, actors, consequences, and implications for democracy, identity, and policymaking.

## The ideologisation and instrumentalisation of history

### Core dynamics
- Every historical narrative performs ideological work: histories select facts, emphasize causation, and impose narrative structures that reflect present values and priorities rather than neutral “truth” alone. Historical narratives thus function as communicative technologies in political discourse, shaping public perceptions and group identities [Historical Narratives and Political Behavior in the US](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm/4769300.pdf?abstractid=4769300&mirid=1) [1]; [Historical Narrative - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/historical-narrative) [3].
- Instrumentalisation occurs when political actors intentionally deploy selective historical interpretations to legitimize policies, mobilize constituencies, or delegitimise opponents. This includes mining “golden-age” tropes, using “bad history” as rhetorical shorthand, and promoting origin myths that justify contemporary agendas [Today's toughest policy problems: how history can help](https://historyandpolicy.org/policy-papers/papers/todays-toughest-policy-problems-how-history-can-help/) [7]; [What is the value of history in policymaking?](https://careforthefuture.exeter.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/Making-History-Work-Report-Final.pdf) [6].

### Political patterns and polarization
- Historical memory is politically polarized. In the U.S., for example, surveys and experimental work demonstrate sharp partisan and racial divides in interpretations of the Civil War, slavery, and the Civil Rights era; conservatives more often emphasize individual agency and discontinuity from the present, while liberals stress structural continuities and historical injustice—differences that correlate with trust in institutions and policy preferences [Historical Narratives and Political Behavior in the US](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm/4769300.pdf?abstractid=4769300&mirid=1) [1].
- Narratives operate as political technologies: they package complex historical interpretation into accessible tropes and symbols that political actors can use in campaigns, educational reforms, commemorations, and foreign policy rhetoric [Constructing political Narratives as a tool of political discourse](https://en.nbpublish.com/library_read_article.php?id=37692) [2].

### Mechanisms of instrumentalisation
- Selection and silencing: deciding which events, victims, or perpetrators are foregrounded or omitted shapes moral and political lessons derived from the past [Public Memory: The Politics of Remembering and Forgetting](https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/rj430k252?locale=en) [8].
- Institutional control: curricula, museums, archives, and official commemorations can standardize certain versions of the past and marginalize alternatives [Why policy needs history (and historians)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/597CC0F217C618D3A7B4102C02BFB50A/S1744133117000433a.pdf/why_policy_needs_history_and_historians.pdf) [5].
- Symbolic artefacts: monuments, statues, and memorials serve as visible, durable claims about what aspects of the past deserve public respect and emulation [Statues and the Shapeshifting of History | National Humanities Center](https://nationalhumanitiescenter.org/humanities-moment/statues-and-the-shapeshifting-of-history/) [23].

### Examples
- Confederate monuments in the United States: erected and defended at different historical moments to assert particular narratives of the Civil War and racial order; debates over their removal reveal the political use of monuments to preserve or contest white supremacist memory and to influence civic identity [Facing History: After Charlottesville](https://www.facinghistory.org/resource-library/after-charlottesville-public-memory-contested-meaning-monuments) [21].
- Russian monument politics: debates over whether to reinstall Lenin-era symbols versus celebrating other historical figures (for example, the Dzerzhinsky vs. Nevsky case) illustrate how competing historical icons can be mobilized to shape political attitudes and legitimacy in the present [Constructing political Narratives as a tool of political discourse](https://en.nbpublish.com/library_read_article.php?id=37692) [2].
- Policy “lessons from history” sometimes become rhetorical devices detached from detailed historical nuance—a warning underscored in policy studies that “newness” rhetoric often throws away usable historical knowledge and replaces it with simplified pasts for political ends [LESSONS FROM HISTORY - UK Parliament](https://www.parliament.uk/documents/post/postpn323.pdf) [4].

## Reclaiming silenced narratives: methods, actors, and limits

### Nature of historical silences
- Silences are not accidental gaps but often result from systematic exclusion—control over archives, institutions, publication channels, and schooling that privileges dominant voices while marginalizing others (racial, gendered, colonial, and classed voices) [Historical silences and the enduring power of counter-storytelling](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03626784.2019.1633735) [13]; [Public Memory: The Politics of Remembering and Forgetting](https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/rj430k252?locale=en) [8].

### Methods for reclamation
- Oral history and community archives: collecting testimony, life stories, and material culture that center previously marginalized experiences (e.g., Indigenous oral traditions, Angel Island detainee accounts), which can reshape local and national narratives by providing first-person evidence and alternative chronologies [Oral History as Tool of Social Justice](https://csw.ucla.edu/2019/02/08/oral-history-as-tool-of-social-justice-challenging-the-status-quo/) [15]; [Native North American Oral Tradition as Identity Reclamation](https://www.drake.edu/media/departmentsoffices/dussj/2021documents/Michalec%20DUSSJ%202021.pdf) [16].
- Archaeological and material reclamation: collaborative archaeology can help communities reclaim ancestral sites, artifacts, and histories suppressed by colonial narratives [Advocating for Archaeology's New Purpose - Sapiens.org](https://www.sapiens.org/archaeology/archaeological-reclamation/) [17].
- Digital technologies and AI: computational methods (NLP, digital archives, mapping) can surface marginalized mentions in digitized records, produce searchable corpora of voices, and support counter-narratives—but ethical constraints and risks of reproducing bias require careful governance [Uncovering Historical Silences with AI](https://www.historica.org/blog/ai-unexpected-role-in-uncovering-historical-silences) [11].
- Cultural production: historical fiction, film, museums, podcasts, and counter-publications expand public access to suppressed stories and can shift popular historical imaginaries [Representing Marginalized Voices in Historical Fiction](http://strangehorizons.com/wordpress/non-fiction/articles/representing-marginalized-voices-in-historical-fiction-and-fantasy/) [12]; [The Transformative Power of Restorative History](https://www.pvamu.edu/blog/opinion-the-transformative-power-of-restorative-history/) [14].

### Scholarly perspectives and debates
- Revisionism vs. restorative work: academic historiography recognizes that revision is permanent—new evidence and perspectives refine understanding. However, “revisionism” is often politically weaponized; legitimate revision aims at greater accuracy and inclusivity, whereas disinformation-driven revisionism seeks ideological erasure or falsification [All History is Revisionist History | NEH](https://www.neh.gov/article/all-history-revisionist-history) [14]; [What Is Revisionist History](https://admisiones.unicah.edu/uploaded-files/NBV42F/3OK067/WhatIsRevisionistHistory.pdf) [9].
- Power and ethics: reclamation requires attention to consent, community leadership, and archival ethics—scholars stress avoiding extractive practices and centering community epistemologies when recovering silenced histories [Confronting our failure of care around legacies in the archives](https://medium.com/on-archivy/confronting-our-failure-of-care-around-the-legacies-of-marginalized-people-in-the-archives-dc4180397280) [4].
- Limits and contestation: reclaiming histories provokes resistance, accusations of politicized “cancel culture,” or reciprocal efforts to weaponize the past—outcomes depend on institutional power, public receptivity, and legal frameworks protecting heritage and free expression [Historical silences and the enduring power of counter-storytelling](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03626784.2019.1633735) [13].

### Examples
- Indigenous oral history movements: amplification of Native narratives through storytelling, digital repatriation, and cultural revitalization projects has reframed public histories of colonization and survival in North America [Native North American Oral Tradition as Identity Reclamation](https://www.drake.edu/media/departmentsoffices/dussj/2021documents/Michalec%20DUSSJ%202021.pdf) [16].
- Angel Island and Chinese immigrant detention: oral testimonies and community archives have countered earlier official narratives that minimized Asian immigrant experiences, reshaping state and public commemoration of immigration history [Oral History as Tool of Social Justice](https://csw.ucla.edu/2019/02/08/oral-history-as-tool-of-social-justice-challenging-the-status-quo/) [15].
- Recovering marginalized scientists and practitioners: projects that reclaim the biography and contributions of excluded groups reshape disciplinary histories and educational curricula [Untold Stories: Reclaiming Histories of Marginalized Scientists](https://ssbbulletin.org/article/id/4457/) [12 in earlier findings].

## Commemorative practices and the shaping of historiography

### Functions of commemoration
- Commemoration (monuments, museums, anniversaries, memorial rituals) does three key things: it selects which pasts are publicly visible, encodes moral lessons and models for civic identity, and anchors historical narratives in place and ritual [Using Commemorative Practices to Teach that History is a Constructed Narrative](https://contestedhistories.org/resources/educational-materials/using-commemorative-practices-to-teach-that-history-is-a-constructed-narrative/) [18]; [The role of memorials in preserving history - the United Nations](https://www.un.org/en/rememberslavery/page/role-memorials-preserving-history) [20].
- Commemorative artifacts are not passive records; they are public declarations about who deserves honor and what civic values should be emulated, and therefore become sites of struggle as values change [Try to Remember: Commemorating and Forgetting the Past](https://bcma.bowdoin.edu/antiquity/try-to-remember-commemorating-and-forgetting/) [5].

### How commemoration shapes historiography
- Monuments and anniversaries institutionalize historical framings that can outlast the original political moment; they can normalize particular causal stories (e.g., heroic nation-building narratives) and marginalize alternative interpretations [Public Monuments and Public Memory - Public Discourse](https://thepublicdiscourse.com/2021/09/78054/) [9].
- Commemoration operates pedagogically (shaping school content), aesthetically (public space design), and politically (legitimising institutions). Thus public memory and formal historiography influence each other in a two-way relationship: academic debates inform public commemorations, which in turn shape public understandings that feed back into scholarly attention [Historical Traces of the Present: The Uses of Commemoration](https://www.jstor.org/stable/41299067) [4].

### Contestation and change
- Monuments acquire "lives" after installation. Their meanings change with shifting contexts: removal, reinterpretation (plaques, added monuments), or contestation (protests, counter-monuments) are common responses when civic values shift [Statues and the Shapeshifting of History | National Humanities Center](https://nationalhumanitiescenter.org/humanities-moment/statues-and-the-shapeshifting-of-history/) [23]; [Deconstructing commemorative narratives: anniversaries study](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/02614367.2023.2215468) [22].
- Counter-commemorations and participatory memorials are strategies to introduce complexity, foreground marginal perspectives, and resist singular heroic narratives—these include community-designed memorials, inclusive museum exhibits, and anniversary events that highlight contested histories [EuroClio SEH-Using-commemorative-practices.pdf](https://www.euroclio.eu/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/SEH-Using-commemorative-practices.pdf) [19].

### Examples
- Transatlantic Slave Trade memorials: international memorials and educational sites (UN-supported initiatives) aim to center victim experiences, educate publics, and influence reparative discourse; memorial design intentionally fosters reflection and moral education rather than glorification [The role of memorials in preserving history - the United Nations](https://www.un.org/en/rememberslavery/page/role-memorials-preserving-history) [20].
- Confederate statue removal and reinterpretation: protests and removals after events such as Charlottesville (2017) led to new plaques, museum contexts, and protests that reframed how local communities interpret Civil War memory [Facing History: After Charlottesville](https://www.facinghistory.org/resource-library/after-charlottesville-public-memory-contested-meaning-monuments) [21].
- Counter-monuments and “defending and de-fencing” strategies: academic and local policy analyses argue for engaged, dialogic approaches to contested monuments (e.g., contextualization, temporary fencing for reflection, community dialogues) rather than simple eradication or preservation as before [Defending and De-fencing: Approaches for Understanding the ...](https://scholarscompass.vcu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1377&context=jstae) [24].

## Actors and institutions shaping memory

### State actors
- Governments use curricula, national museums, public holidays, and monument programs to construct official narratives of national identity. State-sponsored commemoration often seeks legitimacy and cohesion but can marginalize minority experiences [LESSONS FROM HISTORY - UK Parliament](https://www.parliament.uk/documents/post/postpn323.pdf) [4]; [Political Commemoration - PeaceRep](https://peacerep.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/201712_RB_Brown_political-commemoration.pdf) [11 in earlier findings].

### Social movements and communities
- Social movements (civil-rights, Indigenous sovereignty, Black Lives Matter) use counter-memory—protests, counter-monuments, oral history projects—to challenge state narratives and demand recognition and restitution [Event-making the past: Commemorations as social movement practice](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1750698017709871) [13 in earlier findings].

### Media, cultural producers, and tech platforms
- Media frame historical stories for mass publics; films, TV series, podcasts, and social media campaigns can rapidly shift popular memory. Digital platforms have become crucial in surfacing suppressed archives (digitization) but also in amplifying manipulative narratives [Role of Historical Memory in Shaping Contemporary Political ...](https://forthworthjournals.org/journals/index.php/IJHSCA/article/download/106/105/344) [10 in earlier findings]; [Uncovering Historical Silences with AI](https://www.historica.org/blog/ai-unexpected-role-in-uncovering-historical-silences) [11].

### Scholars and heritage professionals
- Historians, museum curators, and archivists mediate between evidence and publics. Scholarship can correct myths, but its public impact depends on translation into pedagogy, exhibits, and media [Why policy needs history (and historians)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/597CC0F217C618D3A7B4102C02BFB50A/S1744133117000433a.pdf/why_policy_needs_history_and_historians.pdf) [5]; [What is the value of history in policymaking?](https://careforthefuture.exeter.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/Making-History-Work-Report-Final.pdf) [6].

## Theoretical lenses and scholarly perspectives

### Memory studies and collective memory
- Collective memory research emphasizes that memory is socially produced and contested; remembering and forgetting are communicative acts shaped by power relations [Public Memory: The Politics of Remembering and Forgetting](https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/rj430k252?locale=en) [8].
- The “politics of forgetting” framework shows how power can intentionally erase or marginalize events to maintain dominance; conversely, counter-memory aims to restore banned or invisible pasts [Public Memory literature] [8].

### Narrative theory and political communication
- Political narrative theory highlights how simplified historical narratives help mobilize emotion and identity, acting as heuristics for political judgment; narrative packaging is central to ideological persuasion [Constructing political Narratives as a tool of political discourse](https://en.nbpublish.com/library_read_article.php?id=37692) [2].

### Historiography and epistemology
- Historiography recognizes revision as a normal process: new sources, theoretical frames, and social perspectives produce different histories. Claims of “revisionism” often signify political conflict rather than purely scholarly dispute [All History is Revisionist History | NEH](https://www.neh.gov/article/all-history-revisionist-history) [14].

## Consequences for contemporary politics and policy

### Democratic legitimacy and social cohesion
- Competing historical narratives can deepen political polarization and influence institutional trust (e.g., divergent Civil War memories correlate with partisan attitudes) [Historical Narratives and Political Behavior in the US](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm/4769300.pdf?abstractid=4769300&mirid=1) [1].
- Inclusive, dialogic commemorative practices can promote reconciliation and civic learning; exclusionary narratives risk social fracture and the legitimation of exclusionary policies [The Power and Promise of Public Memory](https://belonging.berkeley.edu/power-and-promise-public-memory) [10 in earlier findings].

### Policy-making and “lessons from history”
- Historical knowledge adds analytic depth to policy-making, but misuse of history (simplistic analogies, mythic narratives) can produce misguided policies; historians can contribute more usefully when policy processes value historical complexity [Today's toughest policy problems: how history can help](https://historyandpolicy.org/policy-papers/papers/todays-toughest-policy-problems-how-history-can-help/) [7]; [Why policy needs history (and historians)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/597CC0F217C618D3A7B4102C02BFB50A/S1744133117000433a.pdf/why_policy_needs_history_and_historians.pdf) [5].

### Cultural memory and identity formation
- Reclaimed narratives change group self-understanding and can shift public priorities (e.g., recognition of historical injustices spurs reparative debates and curricular change). Commemorative shifts influence who is seen as belonging to the nation and who is deemed peripheral [Competing Historical Narratives: Memory Politics, Identity ...](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0760/12/7/391) [18].

## Recommendations for practice (policy-makers, educators, heritage professionals)

- Approach history as a contested resource: design curricula, museums, and commemorations that emphasize multiplicity, context, and critical thinking rather than single moralistic narratives [Using Commemorative Practices to Teach...](https://contestedhistories.org/resources/educational-materials/using-commemorative-practices-to-teach-that-history-is-a-constructed-narrative/) [18].
- Foster inclusive, community-led reclamation projects: center the voices and governance of communities whose histories are being reclaimed; ensure ethical archival practices and consent in digital projects [Oral History as Tool of Social Justice](https://csw.ucla.edu/2019/02/08/oral-history-as-tool-of-social-justice-challenging-the-status-quo/) [15]; [Advocating for Archaeology's New Purpose - Sapiens.org](https://www.sapiens.org/archaeology/archaeological-reclamation/) [17].
- Use commemoration as dialogue, not monologue: contextualize contested monuments with additional plaques, counter-monuments, or interpretive displays; use anniversary events for plural narratives rather than state monologues [Defending and De-fencing ... VCU](https://scholarscompass.vcu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1377&context=jstae) [24].
- Make historians active partners in policymaking: incorporate historians into advisory roles for policy decisions where historical analogies are invoked; ensure policy institutions demand nuance rather than simple moral lessons from history [LESSONS FROM HISTORY - UK Parliament](https://www.parliament.uk/documents/post/postpn323.pdf) [4]; [Why policy needs history (and historians)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/597CC0F217C618D3A7B4102C02BFB50A/S1744133117000433a.pdf/why_policy_needs_history_and_historians.pdf) [5].
- Regulate and audit digital tools used in reclamation: deploy AI and digital archives with ethical safeguards to avoid reproducing bias and to ensure community control over sensitive data [Uncovering Historical Silences with AI](https://www.historica.org/blog/ai-unexpected-role-in-uncovering-historical-silences) [11].

## Conclusion: memory as a site of politics and possibility
Historical narratives are both instruments of power and opportunities for redress. Ideologisation and instrumentalisation of history are endemic to politics; reclamation and commemoration are the principal arenas where contestation over the past becomes visible. Outcomes depend on institutional balance, civic literacy, and the ethical capacities of historians, cultural workers, and technologists. Thoughtful, inclusive commemorative strategies and rigorous, context-sensitive historical practice can reduce polarizing misuse of the past and open pathways for reconciliation and informed policy.
